tldr: This work pre-extracts the predictive dynamics of a world action model (WAM) into a compact 64-D action-equivalent representation and predicts it online from just an 8-frame causal history, dramatically boosting dynamic conveyor-belt grasp success with zero video generation cost at inference.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of ForeTime-VLA. In the offline teacher stage (left), video latent features including future frames are compressed into an action-equivalent 64-D target. In the online student stage (center), a lightweight encoder predicts the future target, manipulation phase, and time-to-transition from an 8-frame causal history to inject them into the dual pathways of the VLA policy.
overview:
In dynamic manipulation such as picking objects moving on a conveyor belt, success hinges not just on "what is visible right now," but on anticipating the future: when an object will reach the workspace, when to close the gripper, and how to align the end-effector orientation at contact. However, modern Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often fine-tuned solely on the current observation and fail to capture this temporal structure explicitly. Conversely, deploying a video-scale world action model (WAM) directly in a robot's closed-loop control pipeline incurs prohibitive computational cost and latency.

To bridge this gap, the authors asked: "Can we distill the predictive dynamics of a WAM into a lightweight representation without imagining future video frames at inference?" They introduce ForeTime-VLA. During an offline preprocessing phase, a privileged teacher with access to future frames compresses video VAE features into a whitened, action-equivalent 64-D representation. At training time, a small student encoder predicts this future target, the current manipulation phase, and the normalized time-to-transition from just an 8-frame causal history, conditioning both the VLM prefix and the action expert of a $\pi_{0.5}$ base policy.

In real-robot conveyor experiments, ForeTime-VLA achieved an 81.1% stationary grasp success rate and a 58.9% slow-moving grasp success rate, outperforming the baseline $\pi_{0.5}$ by 12.2 and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. Under severe belt-speed stress testing, it completed 11/30 grasps at fast speed, whereas $\pi_{0.5}$ managed only 2/30. The method dramatically cuts contact timing and pose failures while incurring only a 2.5–3% latency overhead.
contributions: Proposed a practical teacher-student distillation framework that captures the predictive dynamics of a video-scale world model (WAM) into an 8-frame causal history encoder without executing the world model at inference.

Designed a dual-path conditioning mechanism that injects predicted future representations, manipulation phases, and time-to-transition into both the slow VLM prefix and the fast action expert of $\pi_{0.5}$.

Extracted action-equivalent future features without representation collapse by combining directional cosine loss, relational Gram-matrix geometry preservation, variance-covariance regularization, and auxiliary action reconstruction.
Demonstrated quantitatively on a real robot that the performance advantage over baselines widens as conveyor belt speed increases and the available interception time shrinks.

sections.heading: Grasping moving objects needs the future: How to deliver world-model insights on a budget
sections.summary: While modern VLAs excel at generating actions from static observations, they struggle with contact timing and end-effector pose prediction in dynamic grasping. This section introduces the concept and contributions of ForeTime-VLA, which distills predictive dynamics from a video world model into a causal history encoder without running the video model at deployment.
sections.details:
Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models such as RT-2, $\pi_0$, and $\pi_{0.5}$ adapt the rich priors of large vision-language foundation backbones to robotic control, generating multimodal, high-dimensional action chunks. However, in dynamic manipulation setups like conveyor belts, looking solely at "what is visible now" is insufficient. The robot must predict future temporal structure: when an object will arrive, when to initiate finger closure, and how to orient the end-effector at the exact moment of contact. Imitation learning alone captures these dynamics only indirectly, suffering from a lack of explicit temporal supervisory signals.

Video-scale world action models (WAMs) can learn these predictive dynamics, but an "imagine-then-act" strategy that generates video frames inside the online control loop is computationally prohibitive. The authors drew inspiration from Fast-WAM's insight: video modeling is most valuable as an auxiliary training signal and can be detached during test-time inference. They designed a framework where the WAM is completely removed at deployment, and a compact predictive representation is inferred strictly from causal history instead.

The main contributions of this work are threefold:
- Established a teacher-student distillation framework driven by an 8-frame causal history encoder, requiring neither future frames nor the WAM at inference.
- Formulated dual-path conditioning that routes predicted future tokens, manipulation phases, and transition horizons to both the VLM prefix and the action expert of $\pi_{0.5}$.
- Demonstrated significant reductions in contact timing and pose errors through offline evaluation and real-robot trials across stationary, moving, and multi-speed stress settings.

captions.F1: Overall system overview. An offline teacher (left) compresses future-aware video features into an action-equivalent 64-D code, which an inference-ready student (center) predicts from an 8-frame history to feed into the dual conditioning pathways of $\pi_{0.5}$.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of VLAs, world models, and distillation: Where this method stands
sections.summary: This section reviews the evolution of VLA foundation models, predictive world models for control, and knowledge distillation techniques. The novelty of ForeTime-VLA lies in distilling future dynamics into a 64-D action-equivalent code for a VLA, bypassing the need for real-time video rollout.
sections.details:
The work situates itself across three primary research areas:

### II-A Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Policies
Models like RT-1, Gato, PaLM-E, RT-2, OpenVLA, and Octo have advanced direct action generation from images and text. More recently, $\pi_0$ and $\pi_{0.5}$ integrated flow matching—a continuous generative framework akin to diffusion models—into dedicated action experts for high-precision control. ForeTime-VLA preserves the continuous flow-matching interface of $\pi_{0.5}$ while introducing predictive temporal supervision during fine-tuning.

### II-B Predictive Representations for Control
Latent world models (e.g., Dreamer) and visual foresight methods anticipate the future to plan actions. Recent systems like UniSim, Fast-WAM, and DECOWAM tackle dynamics at video scale, but online imagination remains computationally heavy. While DECOWAM uses bottleneck distillation from privileged states for legged mobile manipulators, ForeTime-VLA acts complementarily by distilling a compact 64-D future latent into a generalist VLA driven by causal history.

### II-C Knowledge Distillation
Distilling intermediate representations and relational geometry (Relational KD) is well-studied for transferring knowledge from teacher to student. However, intermediate features frequently suffer from rank collapse or complete representation collapse. ForeTime-VLA prevents collapse by coupling directional cosine similarity and Gram-matrix relational geometry with variance-covariance regularization, phase classification, and action reconstruction, preserving only the features essential for manipulation.

sections.heading: How ForeTime-VLA works: Compressing action-equivalent futures and dual-path conditioning
sections.summary: Offline, Wan2.2 video VAE latents and an adapter compress future frame information into an action-reconstructible 64-D code. Online, a student predicts this code, manipulation phase, and time-to-transition from an 8-frame history, injecting them into both the VLM prefix and the action expert of $\pi_{0.5}$.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
At time $t$, the policy observes current image $o_t$, language instruction $\ell$, proprioceptive robot state $s_t$ (26-D), and an 8-step causal history $\mathcal{H}_t$. It outputs a 20-step, 16-D action chunk $a_{t:t+H-1}$. The standard flow-matching loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{flow}}$ of $\pi_{0.5}$ is retained, leaving ground-truth action labels completely unaltered.

### III-B Offline Action-Equivalent Future Teacher
For each training window, the current frame and 8 future offsets $\{2, 4, 7, 9, 12, 14, 17, 19\}$ are sampled. These are encoded with a frozen Wan2.2 video VAE to extract current features $c_t$ (96-D) and future features $f_t$ (96-D). To resolve the lack of diversity in the raw latents, the authors trained an action-equivalent adapter. A privileged teacher encoder maps $(c_t, f_t, s_t)$ and a causal auxiliary encoder maps $(c_t, s_t)$ to 64-D codes, from which a shared action decoder reconstructs the 20-step action chunk. The adapter is trained using teacher-causal alignment, future delta reconstruction, dimensional variance-covariance regularization, and relational geometry preservation. The resulting whitened teacher code $z_t^T$ is precomputed and cached.

### III-C Causal Temporal Student Model
At inference time, the student model takes the past 8 frames of robot states (26-D) and image statistics from two auxiliary cameras (12-D mean and standard deviation). A temporal MLP predicts the compressed future state $\hat{z}_t$ (64-D), 4-class manipulation phase logits $\hat{p}_t$ (approach, grasp/release transition, transport, place/retract), and the normalized time-to-transition $\hat{d}_t \in [0,1]$.

### III-D Dual-Path Conditioning
The predicted signals condition $\pi_{0.5}$ via two parallel paths:
- Slow VLM Path: Four future tokens (2048-D) derived from $\hat{z}_t$ and one phase token derived from phase probabilities are appended to the end of the VLM prefix.
- Fast Action Expert Path: A 1024-D residual vector constructed from $\hat{z}_t$ and $\hat{d}_t$ is added to all suffix tokens and adaptive normalization layers of the action expert.
This conditioning introduces only 1.251M additional parameters, negligible compared to the base backbone (Gemma-2B + 311M expert).

### III-E Training Objectives
Training is performed end-to-end by combining the original action flow loss with a future code cosine loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cos}}$, an intra-batch Gram-matrix geometry loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geom}}$, a phase cross-entropy loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{phase}}$, a Huber loss on time-to-transition $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{time}}$, and an auxiliary action-equivalence loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ae}}$.

captions.F2: The offline action-equivalent future teacher pipeline. A privileged teacher encodes current and future features from a frozen video VAE alongside robot states into a 64-D code. Guided by action reconstruction, variance-covariance regularization, and anti-collapse objectives, whitened target codes $z_t^T$ are precomputed and cached.

sections.heading: Behind the experiments: A strictly deduplicated dataset and standardized protocol
sections.summary: Using 458 deduplicated episodes from a conveyor-belt manipulation dataset, the authors evaluated offline accuracy and inference latency across five model families. Real-robot experiments comprised 90 trials each for stationary and slow-moving grasping, followed by a multi-speed belt stress test of 30 trials per speed.
sections.details:
### IV-A Dataset
An audit of mobile manipulation demonstration data for conveyor picking (boxes, corn, watermelon) revealed 28 exact duplicate files and 1 corrupted file out of 487. Excluding these yielded 458 clean episodes (~1.79 hours at 15 Hz, 96,512 frames), strictly split into 402 training, 31 validation, and 25 test episodes.

### IV-B Compared Baselines and Offline Protocol
As a direct point of comparison, an identical $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone fine-tuned solely on current observations was evaluated. Cross-family baselines included GR00T N1.6-3B, StarVLA QwenGR00T, and SmolVLA-450M. All policies shared identical input/output specifications: three camera streams, 26-D state, 16-D absolute actions, and a 20-step prediction horizon. On 768 matched evaluation windows per split, unnormalized MSE, MAE, and L2 metrics were evaluated with 95% confidence intervals computed via paired bootstrap (20,000 resamples).

### IV-C Real-Robot Protocol
The physical robot evaluation consisted of two primary sessions:
- Session 1: 90 trials per policy across five models on both stationary and slow-moving grasp tasks (450 total trials). In the moving task, failures were classified into four categories: grasp success, early failure, late failure, and contact-pose error.
- Session 2: A belt-speed sensitivity stress test comparing baseline $\pi_{0.5}$ and ForeTime-VLA across three speeds (slow, medium, fast) over 30 trials each (90 total trials).

sections.heading: Results: Big real-robot gains and ablations show why future tokens matter
sections.summary: Offline test MAE decreased by 2.63% and L2 by 3.02%, with the largest gains occurring in end-effector roll, pitch, and yaw. In real-robot trials, slow-moving grasp success jumped from 36.7% to 58.9%, and in fast-belt tests, ForeTime-VLA completed 11 grasps versus only 2 for $\pi_{0.5}$.
sections.details:
### V-A & V-B Offline Action Reconstruction and Model Comparisons
On the test set, ForeTime-VLA reduced MAE from 0.134119 to 0.130593 relative to the baseline $\pi_{0.5}$ (a 2.63% improvement; paired-bootstrap 95% CI: 0.82–4.48%) and cut L2 error by 3.02%. While StarVLA achieved the lowest test MSE (0.237490), ForeTime-VLA secured the top rank across all five models on the less outlier-sensitive MAE and L2 metrics, clearly outperforming other families like GR00T.

### V-C Action Group Breakdown: End-Effector Orientation Gains
Analyzing MAE by action components revealed that the strongest improvement occurred in end-effector rotation (RPY: roll, pitch, yaw), improving by 4.12% on validation and 3.78% on test. This confirms that distilling future and transition supervision enables the policy to align its gripper angle far more accurately at the point of contact.

### V-D Inference-Time Component Ablations
In test-time masking ablations using the same trained checkpoint, masking out the future code $\hat{z}_t$ during the critical grasp/release transition (phase 1) degraded transition MAE by 10.1%, while masking phase and remaining time degraded it by 10.6%. Furthermore, severing either the VLM path or the expert path alone caused noticeable accuracy drops, verifying that the dual pathways operate complementarily.

### V-E Computational Efficiency
Inference latency increased from 66.69 ms to 68.65 ms (+2.93%) on validation and from 66.97 ms to 68.62 ms (+2.46%) on test—an overhead of less than 2 ms. The policy remains substantially faster than GR00T (~132 ms) and StarVLA (~97 ms).

### V-F & V-G Real-Robot Performance: Widening Margins on Moving Targets
Physical robot trials produced remarkable gains:
- Stationary Grasping: ForeTime-VLA achieved 81.1% success (73/90), exceeding the next-best reference StarVLA (68.9%) by 12.2 percentage points and baseline $\pi_{0.5}$ (65.6%) by 15.6 points.
- Slow-Moving Grasping: Success reached 58.9% (53/90), beating baseline $\pi_{0.5}$ (36.7%) by 22.2 points. Late failures fell by 37.5% and contact-pose errors dropped by 57.1%, perfectly mirroring the offline RPY improvements.
- Speed Stress Test: Across slow (19 vs. 13), medium (14 vs. 8), and fast (11 vs. 2) belt speeds, ForeTime-VLA completed 44/90 grasps versus 23/90 for $\pi_{0.5}$—nearly double. The relative advantage grew dramatically at higher speeds, where interception windows are tightest.

sections.heading: Looking ahead: VLAs with future anticipation at zero inference overhead
sections.summary: ForeTime-VLA demonstrates that distilling predictive dynamics from world action models into causal policies is highly effective. With under 3% latency overhead, it substantially improves dynamic grasping, offering a practical blueprint for leveraging world models without running them directly in the control loop.
sections.details:
ForeTime-VLA distills the predictive latent dynamics of a video-scale WAM into a causal flow-matching VLA using action-equivalent codes, manipulation phases, and normalized transition horizons. It yields a 2.63% test MAE and 3.02% test L2 error reduction while keeping latency overhead below 3%. On a physical conveyor belt, it achieved 81.1% stationary and 58.9% slow-moving grasp success, maintaining robust performance (11/30 grasps) in high-speed stress conditions where a standard baseline plummeted to 2/30.

The philosophy of "supervising with a rich world model during training, but extracting its essence with a lightweight causal encoder at runtime" provides a compelling and resource-efficient paradigm for dynamic robotic manipulation.

takeaways: Predictive dynamics from video world models (WAMs) can be successfully transferred to VLAs via compact, action-equivalent 64-D latent codes without running heavy video models at inference.
In dynamic manipulation like conveyor picking, anticipating future states directly translates to sharper end-effector orientation (RPY) tracking and fewer contact-pose failures.
Explicitly predicting structured temporal event signals—such as manipulation phases and time-to-transition—provides strong anchors for continuous action chunk generation.
Dual-path conditioning, which prepends tokens to the slow VLM prefix and injects residuals into the fast action expert, integrates future priors without degrading base model representations.
limitations: Evaluations are restricted to a single conveyor-belt manipulation setup (picking boxes and fruits); generalization across different robot morphologies, camera viewpoints, or long-horizon tasks remains unverified.
The framework relies on a specific offline video backbone (Wan2.2 video VAE / Fast-WAM), leaving performance sensitive to video encoder quality and domain shifts.
StarVLA achieved a lower raw test MSE, suggesting there is still room to improve the mitigation of large outlier residuals.
